claim: The mammalian NF-κB p52:p52 homodimer together with its cofactor Bcl3 activates transcription of κB sites with a central G/C base pair.
source: The mammalian NF-κB p52:p52 homodimer together with its cofactor Bcl3 activates transcription of κB sites with a central G/C base pair (bp), while it is inactive toward κB sites with a central A/T bp.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known property of p52:p52:Bcl3 complex, supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript including luciferase reporter assays.

claim: The p52:p52 homodimer is inactive toward κB sites with a central A/T base pair.
source: The mammalian NF-κB p52:p52 homodimer together with its cofactor Bcl3 activates transcription of κB sites with a central G/C base pair (bp), while it is inactive toward κB sites with a central A/T bp.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by luciferase reporter assays showing reduced transcriptional activity with A/T-centric κB sites.

claim: The crystal structures of p52 in complex with PSel-κB DNA reveal a nearly two-fold widened minor groove in the central region compared to other NF-κB-DNA complex structures.
source: The structures reveal a nearly two-fold widened minor groove in the central region of the DNA as compared to all other currently available NF-κB-DNA complex structures, which have a central A/T bp.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structures presented in the manuscript, with measurements provided in Figure 1I showing minor groove widths of ~7.5 Å.

claim: Free DNAs exhibit distinct preferred conformations as revealed by microsecond MD simulations.
source: Microsecond molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of free DNAs and p52 bound complexes reveal that free DNAs exhibit distinct preferred conformations
evidence: This is demonstrated through MD simulations showing different minor groove widths and conformational states for different DNA sequences.

claim: p52:p52 homodimer induces the least amount of DNA conformational changes when bound to the natural G/C-centric PSel-κB DNA.
source: p52:p52 homodimer induces the least amount of DNA conformational changes when bound to the more transcriptionally active natural G/C-centric PSel-κB
evidence: This is supported by MD simulations comparing free and bound DNA conformations, showing that the G/C-centric DNA maintains similar conformations in both states.

claim: p52:p52 homodimer adopts a closed conformation when bound to mutant A/T and swap DNAs due to their narrowed minor grooves.
source: but adopts closed conformation when bound to the mutant A/T and swap DNAs due to their narrowed minor grooves
evidence: This is demonstrated through MD simulations and structural analysis showing cross-strand contacts by Lys144 in these complexes.

claim: Fast binding kinetics favored by entropy is correlated with higher transcriptional activity.
source: Our binding assays further demonstrate that the fast kinetics favored by entropy is correlated with higher transcriptional activity.
evidence: This is supported by BLI kinetic measurements and ITC thermodynamic data showing that the more transcriptionally active G/C-centric DNA exhibits faster kon and koff rates and positive entropy.

claim: Mammalian NF-κB is assembled combinatorially from five subunits: p50/NF-κB1, p52/NF-κB2, RelA/p65, c-Rel, and RelB.
source: Mammalian NF-κB is assembled combinatorially from five subunits, p50/NF-κB1, p52/NF-κB2, RelA/p65, c-Rel, and RelB, into homo- and heterodimers which bind to specific DNA sequences, known as κB site or κB DNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the NF-κB family composition.

claim: All five NF-κB subunits share a highly conserved Rel homology region (RHR) at their N-termini.
source: All five subunits share a highly conserved region at their N-termini, referred to as the Rel homology region (RHR), and the three-dimensional structures of the RHR are also highly conserved among these proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NF-κB protein structure.

claim: The RHR is approximately 300 residues in length and contains the N-terminal domain (NTD), dimerization domain (DD), and nuclear localization signal (NLS).
source: The RHR is roughly 300 residues in length and contains the N-terminal domain (NTD), dimerization domain (DD), and nuclear localization signal (NLS).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about the RHR domain organization.

claim: The DD alone mediates protein homo- and heterodimerization.
source: The DD alone mediates protein homo- and heterodimerization
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of the dimerization domain.

claim: The NTD and DD together are responsible for DNA binding.
source: the NTD and DD together are responsible for DNA binding
evidence: This is established knowledge about NF-κB DNA binding domains.

claim: The NLS region together with the DD forms the binding sites for IκB proteins.
source: and the NLS region is flexible in solution and together with the DD forms the binding sites for the inhibitor of NF-κB (IκB) proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IκB binding to NF-κB.

claim: p50 and p52 subunits lack a transcriptional activation domain (TAD).
source: The NF-κB proteins can be further divided into two subclasses: the p50 and p52 subunits belong to class I by virtue of their lack of a transcriptional activation domain (TAD).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NF-κB subunit classification.

claim: RelA, c-Rel, and RelB contain a TAD at their C-terminus.
source: The other three subunits, RelA, c-Rel, and RelB, constitute class II with every member containing a TAD at its C-terminus.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NF-κB subunit classification.

claim: Mature p50 and p52 subunits are generated via incomplete proteolysis of their precursor proteins p105 and p100, respectively.
source: Mature p50 and p52 subunits are generated via incomplete proteolysis of their precursor proteins p105 and p100 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about p50 and p52 processing, illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: p50 and p52 possess a short glycine-rich region (GRR) at their C-termini.
source: Therefore, p50 and p52 possess a short glycine-rich region (GRR) at their C-termini.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structure of p50 and p52 proteins.

claim: The initial κB DNA consensus sequence is 5′-G−5G−4G−3R−2N−1W0Y+1Y+2C+3C+4-3′.
source: The initial discovery and characterization of several physiological κB DNAs established the pseudo-symmetric consensus sequence as 5′-G−5G−4G−3R−2N−1W0Y+1Y+2C+3C+4-3′ (Lenardo and Baltimore, 1989), where R=purines, N=any nucleotides, W=either A or T, and Y=pyrimidines.
evidence: This is cited from Lenardo and Baltimore, 1989.

claim: The κB DNA consensus was broadened to 5′-G−5G−4G−3N−2N−1N0N+1N+2C+3C+4-3′ after identification of new NF-κB-DNA binding sites.
source: The subsequent identification of new NF-κB-DNA binding sites broadened the consensus to 5′-G−5G−4G−3N−2N−1N0N+1N+2C+3C+4-3′ (Chen and Ghosh, 1999; Mulero et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from Chen and Ghosh, 1999 and Mulero et al., 2019.

claim: The critical features of the consensus κB DNA sequence are the presence of a series of G and C bases at the 5′ and 3′ ends, respectively, while the bases at the central region can vary.
source: The critical features of the consensus κB DNA sequence are the presence of a series of G and C bases at the 5′ and 3′ ends, respectively, while the bases at the central region can vary.
evidence: This is established knowledge about κB DNA sequence features.

claim: X-ray structures of various NF-κB dimers in complex with different κB DNAs revealed conserved protein-DNA recognition modes.
source: X-ray structures of various NF-κB dimers in complex with different κB DNAs revealed conserved protein-DNA recognition modes for κB DNA that follows the consensus sequence (Müller et al., 1995; Ghosh et al., 1995; Cramer et al., 1997; Chen et al., 1998b; Huang et al., 2001; Moorthy et al., 2007; Fusco et al., 2009; Chen et al., 1998a; Chen et al., 2000; Escalante et al., 2002; Berkowitz et al., 2002; Chen-Park et al., 2002; Panne et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from multiple structural studies.

claim: The RHR of each NF-κB monomer binds to half of a κB DNA, called half-site.
source: The RHR of each monomer binds to half of a κB DNA, called half-site.
evidence: This is established knowledge from structural studies of NF-κB-DNA complexes.

claim: A set of conserved amino acid residues mediate base-specific contacts to the 5′ and 3′ flanking G and C bases in κB DNA.
source: A set of conserved amino acid (aa) residues mediate base-specific contacts to the 5′ and 3′ flanking G and C bases; the inner, more variable bases participate in important, but less base-specific interactions.
evidence: This is established knowledge from structural studies of NF-κB-DNA complexes.

claim: The length of κB DNAs varies from 9 to 11 base pairs.
source: The length of κB DNAs varies from 9 to 11 base pairs (bps).
evidence: This is established knowledge about κB DNA structure.

claim: p50 and p52 subunits bind to a 5 bp half-site (5′-GGGNN-3′).
source: The p50 and p52 subunits bind to a 5 bp half-site (5′-GGGNN-3′)
evidence: This is established knowledge about p50 and p52 DNA binding specificity.

claim: RelA and c-Rel subunits prefer a 4 bp half-site (5′-NNCC-3′).
source: while the RelA and c-Rel subunits prefer a 4 bp half-site (5′-NNCC-3′).
evidence: This is established knowledge about RelA and c-Rel DNA binding specificity.

claim: p50:p50 and p52:p52 homodimers prefer an 11 bp κB site comprising two 5 bp half-sites separated by a central bp.
source: Following this binding pattern, both the p50:p50 and p52:p52 homodimers prefer an 11 bp κB site comprising of two 5 bp half-sites separated by a central bp (5+1+5 bps), such as the IL-6-κB site (5′-GGGATTTTCCC-3′).
evidence: This is established knowledge about p50 and p52 homodimer DNA binding preferences.

claim: RelA:RelA and c-Rel:c-Rel homodimers bind 9 bp κB sites containing two 4 bp half-sites.
source: On the other hand, RelA:RelA and c-Rel:c-Rel homodimers bind 9 bp κB sites containing two 4 bp half-sites (4+1+4 bps), such as the IL-8-κB site (5′-GGAATTTCC-3′).
evidence: This is established knowledge about RelA and c-Rel homodimer DNA binding preferences.

claim: Heterodimers containing one p50 or p52 subunit recognize a 10 bp κB site.
source: Heterodimers containing one p50 or p52 subunit, such as p50:RelA and p52:RelB, recognize a 10 bp κB site (5+1+4 bps), that is, the HIV-κB site (5′-GGGACTTTCC-3′) and IFN-β-κB site (5′-GGGAAATTCC-3′)
evidence: This is established knowledge about NF-κB heterodimer DNA binding preferences.

claim: The central bp of κB DNA lies at the pseudo-dyad axis of the NF-κB dimer and is not directly contacted by the protein.
source: in which the central bp lies at the pseudo-dyad axis of the dimer and is not directly contacted by the protein.
evidence: This is established knowledge from structural studies of NF-κB-DNA complexes.

claim: Genome-wide studies revealed that NF-κB associates not only with consensus κB DNAs, but also with sequences containing only one half-site consensus, and even some sequences with no consensus.
source: Genome-wide NF-κB-DNA motif identification studies revealed that NF-κB associates not only with consensus κB DNAs, but also with sequences containing only one half-site consensus, and even some sequences with no consensus (Lim et al., 2007; Martone et al., 2003; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from genome-wide studies by Lim et al., 2007; Martone et al., 2003; Zhao et al., 2014.

claim: The binding affinity displayed by various NF-κB dimers for distinct κB DNAs does not necessarily correlate with gene regulation in vivo.
source: The binding affinity displayed by various NF-κB dimers for distinct κB DNAs does not necessarily correlate with what occurs during regulation of gene expression in vivo.
evidence: This is established knowledge from in vitro and in vivo studies of NF-κB function.

claim: p50:RelA heterodimer binds tightly to most κB DNAs.
source: For example, the p50:RelA heterodimer binds tightly to most κB DNAs
evidence: This is established knowledge from in vitro binding studies.

claim: RelA:RelA and c-Rel:c-Rel homodimers bind many κB DNA sequences with relatively low affinity.
source: whereas RelA:RelA and c-Rel:c-Rel homodimers bind many of the same sequences with relatively low affinity.
evidence: This is established knowledge from in vitro binding studies.

claim: Mice lacking c-Rel exhibit defects in IL-2 and IL-12 expression.
source: However, detailed genetic experiments have shown that some genes are activated only in the presence of one or a subset of NF-κB subunits, such as mice lacking c-Rel exhibit defects in IL-2 and IL-12 expression (Köntgen et al., 1995; Hoffmann et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from genetic studies by Köntgen et al., 1995 and Hoffmann et al., 2003.

claim: RelA and p50 dimers repress the expression of nrp1 gene, which is essential for osteoclast differentiation.
source: The RelA and p50 dimers have been shown to repress the expressions of nrp1 gene, which is essential for osteoclast differentiation, and the interferon-stimulated response element, respectively (Cheng et al., 2011; Hayashi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Cheng et al., 2011 and Hayashi et al., 2012.

claim: Structural and biochemical analyses revealed the existence of a large number of κB DNAs that display relatively similar affinities compared with κB consensus even though they lack one consensus half-site entirely.
source: Structural and biochemical analyses of NF-κB-DNA binding have also revealed the existence of a large number of κB DNAs that display relatively similar affinities compared with κB consensus even though they lack one consensus half-site entirely (Ghosh et al., 2012; Siggers et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Ghosh et al., 2012 and Siggers et al., 2011.

claim: NF-κB p52 is generated from the precursor protein p100, a tightly regulated process that requires specific stimuli.
source: NF-κB p52 is generated from the precursor protein p100 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), a tightly regulated process that requires specific stimuli.
evidence: This is established knowledge about p52 processing.

claim: Unregulated p100 processing into p52 results in multiple myeloma and other lymphoid malignancies.
source: Unregulated p100 processing into p52 results in multiple myeloma and other lymphoid malignancies, which is detrimental to normal cellular function (Courtois and Gilmore, 2006; Annunziata et al., 2007; Keats et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from Courtois and Gilmore, 2006; Annunziata et al., 2007; Keats et al., 2007.

claim: The p52:p52 homodimer can sense a single bp change from G/C to A/T at the central position of a κB DNA.
source: We previously demonstrated that the p52:p52 homodimer could sense a single bp change from G/C to A/T at the central position of a κB DNA (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from the authors' previous work, Wang et al., 2012.

claim: When bound to G/C-centric DNA, p52:p52:Bcl3 complex activates transcription by recruiting histone acetyltransferases.
source: The p52:p52 homodimer binds both κB DNAs; but only in the case of the G/C-centric DNA, p52:p52 homodimer can associate with its specific cofactor Bcl3 (p52:p52:Bcl3 complex) and activate transcription by recruiting histone acetyltransferases.
evidence: This is cited from the authors' previous work.

claim: When bound to A/T-centric DNA, the p52:p52:Bcl3 complex represses gene transcription through the recruitment of histone deacetylases.
source: When bound to the A/T-centric DNA, the same p52:p52:Bcl3 complex represses gene transcription through the recruitment of histone deacetylases.
evidence: This is cited from the authors' previous work.

claim: The transcriptional activity of the RelA:RelA homodimer differs when bound to IP-10-κB DNA versus MCP-1-κB DNA.
source: Leung et al. reported that the transcriptional activity of the RelA:RelA homodimer upon binding to the IP-10-κB DNA (5′-GGGAAATTCC-3′) and the MCP-1-κB DNA (5′-GGGAATTTCC-3′) are different; a single bp difference between the A-centric IP-10-κB and T-centric MCP-1-κB DNAs alters the genes' responsiveness to RelA (Leung et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from Leung et al., 2004.

claim: Crystal structures of p52:p52 homodimer in complex with natural G/C-centric PSel-κB DNA were determined.
source: In the present study, we determined the crystal structures of the p52:p52 homodimer in complex with the natural G/C-centric PSel-κB DNA (5′-GGGGTGACCCC-3′)
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, with crystallographic data presented in Table 1.

claim: Crystal structures of p52:p52 homodimer in complex with PSel (mutant A/T-centric) DNA were determined.
source: and two related DNAs where the central three positions were varied, named as PSel (mutant A/T-centric) (5′-GGGGTAACCCC-3′)
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, with crystallographic data presented in Table 1.

claim: Crystal structures of p52:p52 homodimer in complex with PSel (−1/+1 swap) DNA were determined.
source: and PSel (−1/+1 swap) (5′-GGGGAGTCCCC-3′).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, with crystallographic data presented in Table 1.

claim: PSel is a known target gene regulated by the p52:p52:Bcl3 complex in cells.
source: PSel is a known target gene regulated by the p52:p52:Bcl3 complex in cells (Pan and McEver, 1995; Wang et al., 2012)
evidence: This is cited from Pan and McEver, 1995 and Wang et al., 2012.

claim: PSel (mutant A/T-centric) and (−1/+1 swap) κB DNAs reduced the transcriptional activity significantly.
source: however, the PSel (mutant A/T-centric) and (−1/+1 swap) κB DNAs reduced the transcriptional activity significantly.
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 1B.

claim: All three p52:p52-PSel DNA structures revealed a widening of the DNA minor groove in the central region compared to previously known structures of NF-κB-(A/T-centric)-DNA complexes.
source: All three structures revealed a widening of the DNA minor groove in the central region compared to all previously known structures of NF-κB-(A/T-centric)-DNA complexes.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures with measurements provided in Figure 1I.

claim: MD simulations showed that the more transcriptionally active Psel (natural G/C-centric) κB DNA has an intrinsically widened minor groove.
source: MD simulations showed free DNAs exist in distinct preferred conformations, and the p52:p52 homodimer induces the least amount of conformational changes on the more transcriptionally active Psel (natural G/C-centric) κB DNA which has an intrinsically widened minor groove.
evidence: This is demonstrated through MD simulations of free and bound DNA conformations.

claim: In vitro experiments demonstrated that the binding kinetics, rather than the binding affinity, is correlated with transcriptional activities.
source: In vitro experiments further demonstrated that the binding kinetics, rather than the binding affinity, is correlated with their transcriptional activities.
evidence: This is demonstrated through BLI kinetic measurements and ITC thermodynamic data correlated with luciferase reporter assays.

claim: The natural G/C-centric PSel luciferase reporter was activated by endogenous NF-κB with LPS stimulation and Bcl3 co-expression.
source: The natural PSel luciferase reporter could be activated by endogenous NF-κB with co-expression of Bcl3 followed by lipopolysaccharide stimulation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 1A.

claim: PSel (mutant A/T-centric) showed twofold reduced reporter activity compared to natural PSel-κB.
source: PSel (mutant A/T-centric) showed twofold reduced reporter activity
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PSel (−1/+1 swap) showed drastically reduced transcriptional activity compared to natural PSel-κB.
source: while both PSel (−1/+1 swap) and MHC-κB showed drastically reduced transcriptional activity as compared to the natural PSel-κB (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 1B.

claim: MHC-κB showed drastically reduced transcriptional activity compared to natural PSel-κB.
source: while both PSel (−1/+1 swap) and MHC-κB showed drastically reduced transcriptional activity as compared to the natural PSel-κB (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The bp identity at all three positions in the central region is critical in determining transcriptional activity of the p52:p52:Bcl3 complex.
source: These results suggest that the bp identity at all three positions in the central region is critical in determining transcriptional activity of the p52:p52:Bcl3 complex, which is in line with our previous study that the central bp of κB DNAs plays critical roles in transcriptional regulation (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the luciferase reporter assay results and cited from Wang et al., 2012.

claim: All three PSel-κB DNAs exhibited a distinct widening of the minor groove at the two base-steps around the central position 0 (−1 to 0 and 0 to +1), with width of ~7.5 Å.
source: One is that all three PSel-κB DNAs exhibited a distinct widening of the minor groove at the two base-steps around the central position 0 (−1 to 0 and 0 to +1), with width of ~7.5 Å (Figure 1E–G1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structures with measurements shown in Figure 1E-G and quantified in Figure 1I.

claim: The A/T-centric κB DNAs κB-33 and κB-55 have significantly compressed minor groove in both their bound and free states compared to an ideal B-form DNA.
source: In comparison, the A/T-centric κB DNAs studied earlier, κB-33 (5′-GGAAATTTCC-3′) (Chen et al., 1998a; Huang et al., 2005) and another one that we now name κB-55 (5′-GGGAATTCCC-3′) (Moorthy et al., 2007; Fusco et al., 2009), have significantly compressed minor groove in both their bound and free states as compared to an ideal B-form DNA (Figure 1I; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is observed by comparing crystal structures and measurements shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-B, with citations to Chen et al., 1998a; Huang et al., 2005; Moorthy et al., 2007; Fusco et al., 2009.

claim: Compressed minor groove width is a common feature of all A/T-centric κB DNAs bound to NF-κB dimers.
source: Compressed minor groove width is a common feature of all A/T-centric κB DNAs bound to NF-κB dimers which is remarkably different from the minor groove width of the PSel-κB DNAs seen in the present structures (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is observed by comparing multiple crystal structures summarized in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Superposition of the p52:p52 homodimer in the MHC-κB and natural PSel-κB complexes aligned by the DDs reveals large rigid body movement of NTDs with rotation of ~20° and translation along rotation axis of ~1.4 Å.
source: Superposition of the p52:p52 homodimer in the MHC-κB and natural PSel-κB complexes aligned by the DDs reveals large rigid body movement of NTDs with rotation of ~20° and translation along rotation axis of ~1.4 Å (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is observed by structural comparison shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The rigid body movement of NTDs results in shifting of the NTD along PSel DNA toward its flanks by ~13 Å for both sides.
source: This results in shifting of the NTD along PSel DNA toward its flanks by ~13 Å for both sides.
evidence: This is observed by structural comparison shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The minor groove of the MHC-κB DNA at the central segment is compressed like all other NF-κB-DNA complexes.
source: In addition, the minor groove of the MHC-κB DNA at the central segment is compressed like all other NF-κB-DNA complexes indicated above (Figure 1I; Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure with measurements shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The short p52 protein (aa 1–327) only co-crystallized with a 13 bp PSel (mutant A/T-centric) DNA but not the (natural G/C-centric) or (−1/+1 swap) DNAs in any lengths.
source: This short p52 protein only co-crystallized with a 13 bp PSel (mutant A/T-centric) DNA but not the (natural G/C-centric) or (−1/+1 swap) DNAs in any lengths.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from crystallization trials.

claim: The conformation of the short p52 (aa 1–327) complex with 13 bp PSel (mutant A/T-centric) DNA is nearly identical to p52-MHC-κB complex with minor groove width less than 4 Å at the central position.
source: The conformation of this complex is nearly identical to p52-MHC-κB complex with minor groove width less than 4 Å at the central position (Figure 2B; Figure 1I; Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is observed by structural comparison shown in Figure 2B, Figure 1I, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Both the DNA and protein lengths play significant roles in determining the structure of the complex.
source: This crystal with short p52 is in a different crystal form compared to the three structures with the long p52, and it is also in a different crystal form compared to the MHC-κB DNA complex, suggesting that crystal packing is unlikely to be the main cause of the structural differences, and that both the DNA and protein lengths play significant roles.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing crystal structures with different protein and DNA lengths.

claim: The short p52 protein (aa 1–327) failed to interact with Bcl3.
source: As discussed above, the short p52 protein (aa 1–327) failed to interact with Bcl3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–H), partly due to the lack of the GRR.
evidence: This is demonstrated by BLI and size exclusion chromatography experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-H.

claim: The widening of the minor groove propagates from the central position to all four base steps on both sides with values around 5–6 Å.
source: The widening of the minor groove propagates from the central position to all four base steps on both sides with values around 5–6 Å (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures with measurements shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The widening and deepening of the DNA grooves have significant impact on protein-DNA interactions, most significantly the loss of cross-strand base contacts by Arg52.
source: This widening and the consequent deepening of the major groove have significant impact on protein-DNA interactions. The most significant of which is the loss of cross-strand base contacts by Arg52 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Cross-strand contacts between the homologous Arg and DNA are observed in all other A/T-centric NF-κB-DNA structures.
source: The cross-strand contacts between the homologous Arg (Arg54 in p50 and Arg33 in RelA) and DNA are observed in all other A/T-centric NF-κB-DNA structures (Figure 3B; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is observed by comparing multiple crystal structures shown in Figure 3B and Supplementary file 3.

claim: In the 18 bp long PSel-κB DNA complexes, the NH1 and NH2 groups of Arg52 form H-bonds with both O6 and N7 groups of G at ±3.
source: In the 18 bp long PSel-κB DNA complexes, the NH1 and NH2 groups of Arg52 form H-bonds with both O6 and N7 groups of G at ±3.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures.

claim: Arg52 in the complex with the short 13 bp PSel (mutant A/T-centric) or the MHC-κB DNA only hydrogen bonds with the O6 group, but not the N7, of G at ±3.
source: The same Arg52 in the complex with the short 13 bp PSel (mutant A/T-centric) or the MHC-κB DNA only hydrogen bonds with the O6 group, but not the N7, of G at ±3.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures.

claim: The p52:52 homodimer displays substantial asymmetry with the NTDs rotating from each other by ~6° when the DD of the two monomers are superposed.
source: Moreover, the p52:52 homodimer also displays substantial asymmetry. With the DD of the two monomers in superposition, the NTDs rotate from each other by ~6° (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The interdomain interaction is extensive in monomer I compared to that in monomer II.
source: The interdomain interaction is extensive in monomer I compared to that in monomer II (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In the PSel-κB complex, the side chains of Lys221, Arg52, Arg54, and His62 in p52 monomer I make direct base-specific contacts to four consecutive G(s) from +2 to +5 positions.
source: In the PSel-κB complex, the side chains of Lys221, Arg52, Arg54, and His62 in p52 monomer I make direct base-specific contacts to four consecutive G(s) from +2 to +5 positions (Figure 3E, left).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures shown in Figure 3E.

claim: p52 monomer II makes contact with only three G(s) from position −3 to −5.
source: p52 monomer II makes contact with only three G(s) from position −3 to −5 (Figure 3E, right).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Only Lys221 in monomer I makes specific contacts with G at position +2.
source: The conformation of loop L3 in the two p52 monomers is different; consequently, only Lys221 in monomer I makes specific contacts with G at position +2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There is a unique basic segment in p52, a peptide-rich in basic residues (K179ELKK), located near the end of helix α2.
source: In addition, there is a unique basic segment in p52, a peptide-rich in basic residues (K179ELKK), located near the end of helix α2 (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is observed by sequence alignment shown in Figure 3G.

claim: These basic residues possibly mediate long-range electrostatic interactions with the negatively charged DNA backbone which might pull the DNA strands away from each other toward the p52 protein.
source: These basic residues possibly mediate long-range electrostatic interactions with the negatively charged DNA backbone which might pull the DNA strands away from each other toward the p52 protein (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is speculated based on structural observations shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Throughout MD simulations, PSel (natural G/C-centric) largely maintained its widened minor groove at the central 0 position.
source: Throughout our simulations PSel (natural G/C-centric) largely maintained its widened minor groove at the central 0 position
evidence: This is demonstrated by MD simulations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The minor groove in PSel (mutant A/T-centric) narrowed slightly during MD simulations.
source: while the minor groove in PSel (mutant A/T-centric) narrowed slightly
evidence: This is demonstrated by MD simulations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: PSel (−1/+1 swap) displayed a significantly narrowed minor groove during MD simulations, which became similar to that of MHC-κB DNA.
source: PSel (−1/+1 swap) displayed a significantly narrowed minor groove, which became similar to that of MHC-κB DNA recorded in the simulations (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MD simulations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The swap of T and A at ±1 positions reverses the geometric conformation of bps at both positions.
source: The swap of T and A at ±1 positions reverses the geometric conformation of bps at both positions (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MD simulations shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The swaps exchange pyrimidines and purines at ±1 positions, forcing the swapped bps to adopt an opposite shear and buckle direction to optimize base stacking with neighboring bps.
source: Specifically, these swaps exchange pyrimidines and purines at ±1 positions, forcing the swapped bps to adopt an opposite shear and buckle direction to optimize base stacking with neighboring bps compared to those on the non-swapped DNAs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MD simulations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The thymines at both ±1 positions slide and tilt toward the minor groove simultaneously, narrowing the central minor grooves in the swap DNA.
source: The thymines at both positions slide and tilt toward the minor groove simultaneously, narrowing the central minor grooves (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MD simulations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The A:T bp at 0 position shows large shear, buckle, and opening, forcing a register toward the minor groove in the curvature of free A/T-centric DNAs.
source: The A:T bp at 0 position shows large shear, buckle, and opening, forcing a register toward the minor groove in the curvature of free A/T-centric DNAs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MD simulations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Having successive A:T is likely to reduce the intrinsic minor groove width.
source: Collectively, we conclude that having successive A:T is likely to reduce the intrinsic minor groove width.
evidence: This is inferred from MD simulation results.

claim: The finding that successive A:T reduces minor groove width is in line with observations of a compressed minor groove of free κB-33 DNA or the bending into the minor groove from continuous A:T in A-tract DNAs.
source: Our finding is in line with the observations of a compressed minor groove of free κB-33 DNA or the bending into the minor groove from continuous A:T in A-tract DNAs (Barbic et al., 2003; Huang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from Barbic et al., 2003 and Huang et al., 2005.

claim: Upon binding to p52, the −1/+1 swap DNA experiences more disruptive conformational change than the natural G/C-centric PSel-κB.
source: Comparison of MD simulations and crystal structures suggests that upon binding to p52, the −1/+1 swap DNA experiences more disruptive conformational change than the natural G/C-centric PSel-κB (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing MD simulations and crystal structures shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: p52:p52 homodimer adopts a specific conformation with a nearly fixed inter-monomer distance upon binding to κB DNAs.
source: It appears that p52:p52 homodimer adopts a specific conformation with a nearly fixed inter-monomer distance upon the binding to κB DNAs, such that it tears the central part of −1/+1 swap DNA into a favored binding conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from structural and MD simulation analysis.

claim: p52:p52 binds all three PSel-κB DNA variants with similar binding affinities (Kd) in the range of approximately 40–90 nM.
source: Isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) reveals that p52:p52 binds all three PSel-κB DNA variants with similar binding affinities (Kd) in the range of approximately 40–90 nM
evidence: This is demonstrated by ITC experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: p52:p52 binds MHC-κB DNA much tighter than the PSel-κB DNA variants.
source: whereas it binds MHC-κB DNA much tighter (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ITC experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Binding of p52 to the natural G/C-centric PSel-κB DNA is associated with a large increase in entropy (ΔS) and a moderate decrease in enthalpy (ΔH).
source: However, binding of p52 to the natural G/C-centric PSel-κB DNA is associated with a large increase in entropy (ΔS) and a moderate decrease in enthalpy (ΔH).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ITC experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The binding of p52:p52 to the MHC and mutant A/T-centric PSel DNAs showed a much larger decrease in enthalpy.
source: On the other hand, the binding to the MHC and mutant A/T-centric PSel DNAs showed a much larger decrease in enthalpy.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ITC experiments shown in Figure 5B and 5D.

claim: The binding of p52:p52 homodimer to the G/C-centric κB DNA is favored more by entropy, whereas the binding to the A/T-centric DNA is driven by enthalpy alone.
source: These results suggest that the binding of p52:p52 homodimer to the G/C-centric κB DNA is favored more by entropy, whereas the binding to the A/T-centric DNA is driven by enthalpy alone.
evidence: This is inferred from ITC experimental results.

claim: Skp2-κB DNA is present in the promoter of S-phase kinase-associated protein 2 (Skp2) and is regulated by the p52:p52 homodimer and Bcl3.
source: Skp2-κB DNA is present in the promoter of S-phase kinase-associated protein 2 (Skp2) and it is also regulated by the p52:p52 homodimer and Bcl3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A; Barré and Perkins, 2007; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Barré and Perkins, 2007 and Wang et al., 2012, and demonstrated by luciferase assays in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The Kd as well as relative contributions of entropy and enthalpy to the binding to Skp2 and −1/+1 swap PSel DNAs are similar.
source: The Kd as well as relative contributions of entropy and enthalpy to the binding to Skp2 and −1/+1 swap PSel DNAs are similar (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ITC experiments shown in Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: DNA sequence and conformational differences lead p52 to bind DNAs through different thermodynamic binding processes.
source: These results suggest that DNA sequence and conformational differences lead p52 to bind DNAs through different thermodynamic binding processes.
evidence: This is inferred from ITC experimental results.

claim: The binding of more transcriptionally active natural G/C-centric PSel showed a higher association (kon) and dissociation rate (koff) than the other two variants and MHC-κB DNAs.
source: The binding of more transcriptionally active natural G/C-centric PSel showed a higher association (kon) and dissociation rate (koff) than the other two variants and MHC-κB DNAs (Figure 6A–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BLI experiments shown in Figure 6A-E.

claim: The more transcriptionally active natural G/C-centric Skp2 showed a faster kinetics than its mutant A/T-centric, especially the koff.
source: Consistently, in the case of Skp2-κB DNA, the more transcriptionally active natural G/C-centric Skp2 showed a faster kinetics than its mutant A/T-centric, especially the koff (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BLI experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Only the recombinant phospho-mimetic Bcl3 from E. coli forms ternary complex with p52:p52 homodimer and κB DNA.
source: In agreement with our previous study, only the recombinant phospho-mimetic Bcl3 from Escherichia coli forms ternary complex with p52:p52 homodimer and κB DNA (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Wang et al., 2017.

claim: Both recombinant WT and phospho-mimetic Bcl3 protein interact with p52 with similar kinetics.
source: Both recombinant WT and phospho-mimetic Bcl3 protein interact with p52 with similar kinetics (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–C)
evidence: This is demonstrated by BLI experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: The p52:p52:WT-Bcl3 complex does not bind DNAs.
source: however, the p52:p52:WT-Bcl3 complex does not bind DNAs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BLI experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D-E.

claim: The binding of p52:p52:phospho-Bcl3 with the natural G/C-centric PSel DNA exhibited both higher kon and koff.
source: The binding of p52:p52:phospho-Bcl3 with the natural G/C-centric PSel DNA exhibited both higher kon and koff (Figure 6F–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BLI experiments shown in Figure 6F-J.

claim: The binding kinetics of p52:p52 homodimer alone versus p52:p52:Bcl3 complex follows the same trend.
source: Overall, the binding kinetics of p52:p52 homodimer alone versus p52:p52:Bcl3 complex follows the same trend.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing BLI experimental results.

claim: A comparison of binding affinity, association, and dissociation rates shows a correlation between transcriptional output and the dissociation rate.
source: Moreover, a comparison of binding affinity, association, and dissociation rates with respect to the more transcriptionally active PSel and Skp2-κB sites shows a correlation between transcriptional output and the dissociation rate.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing BLI kinetic data with luciferase reporter assay results shown in Figure 6K and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The slower the koff, the lower the reporter activities for both (p52:p52)-DNA and (p52:p52:Bcl3)-DNA complexes.
source: The slower the koff, the lower the reporter activities for both (p52:p52)-DNA and (p52:p52:Bcl3)-DNA complexes (Figure 6K; Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing BLI kinetic data with luciferase reporter assay results shown in Figure 6K and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Transcriptional activity may have a closer link to the binding kinetics rather than the thermodynamic stability of the complex.
source: Therefore, transcriptional activity may have a closer link to the binding kinetics rather than the thermodynamic stability of the complex.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing ITC and BLI data with transcriptional activity measurements.

claim: Upon p52:p52 homodimer binding, the central minor grooves of all three DNAs narrowed during MD simulations.
source: Upon p52:p52 homodimer binding, the central minor grooves of all three DNAs narrowed, resulting in a consistent trend as seen in the free form (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MD simulations shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The p52:p52 subunits bound to −1/+1 swap DNA adopt a closed conformation where the two segments bound to the central minor groove appear to clamp the DNA.
source: Adapting to the width of the DNA central minor groove, the p52:p52 subunits bound to −1/+1 swap DNA adopt a closed conformation where the two segments bound to the central minor groove appear to clamp the DNA, in contrast to their more open conformation when bound to the natural G/C-centric DNA
evidence: This is demonstrated by MD simulations shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The NTD of p52:p52 subunits could make contacts across the central minor grooves when bound to mutant A/T-centric and −1/+1 swap DNAs.
source: Notably, we found that the NTD of p52:p52 subunits could make contacts across the central minor grooves when bound to mutant A/T-centric and −1/+1 swap DNAs (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MD simulations shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The clamping conformation enables Lys144 to form cross-strand binding that engages the phosphates at −3/+3 positions in the opposite DNA strands in the mutant A/T and −1/+1 swap DNAs.
source: Specifically, the clamping conformation enables Lys144 to form cross-strand binding that engages the phosphates at −3/+3 positions in the opposite DNA strands in the mutant A/T and −1/+1 swap DNAs (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MD simulations shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Cross-strand contacts by Lys144 were approximately five times more frequent in −1/+1 swap DNA and three times more frequent in mutant A/T-centric DNA than in the natural G/C-centric DNA.
source: These cross-strand contacts, while recorded in all three protein-DNA complexes, were most frequently observed in the −1/+1 swap and mutant A/T-centric DNAs. Specifically, they were approximately five and three times more frequent than in the natural G/C-centric DNA, respectively (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MD simulations shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The p52K144A mutant binds to all three PSel-κB DNAs with weaker affinity compared to the WT p52.
source: Overall, the p52K144A mutant binds to all three PSel-κB DNAs with weaker affinity compared to the WT p52 (Figure 8; Figure 6), likely due to the completely abolished Lys144 cross-strand contacts.
evidence: This is demonstrated by BLI experiments shown in Figure 8 compared to Figure 6.

claim: Dissociation of all three DNAs from p52K144A mutant is sped up relative to the WT p52, with the most prominent change recorded for −1/+1 swap.
source: Consistent with the simulation analysis, dissociation of all three DNAs from p52K144A mutant is sped up relative to the WT p52, with the most prominent change recorded for −1/+1 swap.
evidence: This is demonstrated by BLI experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: The p52K144A mutation does not affect its interaction with Bcl3.
source: The p52K144A mutant was expressed and purified to similar purity as the WT p52 protein, and the mutation does not affect its interaction with Bcl3 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BLI and size exclusion chromatography experiments shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: All three PSel-κB DNA variants bound to the long p52:p52 homodimer are similar but are distinct from all previously known complexes between κB DNAs and six other NF-κB dimers.
source: Structures presented in this study show that the conformations of all three PSel-κB DNA variants bound to the long p52:p52 homodimer are similar but are distinct from all previously known complexes between κB DNAs and six other NF-κB dimers (p50:p50, p50:RelA, p50:RelB, RelA:RelA, c-Rel:c-Rel, and p52:RelB).
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural comparison of the current structures with previously published structures.

claim: A compressed minor groove in the central region of the DNA is a key feature of NF-κB-DNA complexes.
source: It was noted earlier a compressed minor groove in the central region of the DNA is a key feature of NF-κB-DNA complexes.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous structural studies.

claim: The more transcriptionally active natural PSel-κB DNA appears to maintain similar conformational and dynamic states in free and bound forms.
source: And notably, the more transcriptionally active natural PSel-κB DNA appears to maintain similar conformational and dynamic states in free and bound forms.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing MD simulations of free and bound DNA conformations.

claim: The GRR region of the p52 protein seems to play an important role in determining the conformation of the κB DNA.
source: The current structures also demonstrate a correlation between the p52 protein length and the conformation of the κB DNA. The GRR region of the p52 protein, which was not included in any previous NF-κB structural studies, seems to play an important role.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing structures with different p52 protein lengths.

claim: No electron density was observed for the GRR region in the current structures.
source: However, no electron density was observed for the GRR region in the current structures.
evidence: This is an observation from the crystal structures.

claim: p52:p52 homodimer binds to MHC-κB with the highest affinity but it is not a transcriptional activation competent complex.
source: The p52:p52 homodimer binds to MHC-κB with the highest affinity but it is not a transcriptional activation competent complex.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ITC and luciferase reporter assays.

claim: In the complex between p52:p52 and natural G/C-centric DNA, both the DNA and protein most likely preserve their native states.
source: Thus, in the complex between p52:p52 and natural G/C-centric DNA, both the DNA and protein most likely preserve their native states.
evidence: This is inferred from MD simulations and structural analysis.

claim: p52:p52 complexes with the mutant A/T-centric or −1/+1 swap DNAs likely involve rigidification of protein-DNA contacts, requiring some structural reorganizations in both molecules.
source: In contrast, p52:p52 complexes with the mutant A/T-centric or−1/+1 swap DNAs likely involve rigidification of protein-DNA contacts, requiring some structural reorganizations in both molecules, resulting in more enthalpically stable complexes and slower association and dissociation rates.
evidence: This is inferred from ITC, BLI, and MD simulation data.

claim: Rapid association and dissociation are favored by entropy, whereas slow association and dissociation are guided by enthalpy.
source: Our observations are consistent with other studies which have shown that rapid association and dissociation are favored by entropy, whereas slow association and dissociation are guided by enthalpy (Baerga-Ortiz et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from Baerga-Ortiz et al., 2004.

claim: Differential affinity has been shown to be critical in many cases of eukaryotic transcription.
source: Indeed, in many cases of eukaryotic transcription differential affinity has been shown to be critical (Sekiya et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Sekiya et al., 2009.

claim: TFs are known to bind free DNA or nucleosome with distinct kinetics.
source: TFs are also known to bind free DNA or nucleosome with distinct kinetics (Donovan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from Donovan et al., 2019.

claim: Receptor-ligand interactions, T cell activation, and potency of bacterial toxins are guided by the half-life of key complexes.
source: For instance, receptor-ligand interactions, T cell activation, and potency of bacterial toxins are guided by the half-life of key complexes (Corzo, 2006; González et al., 2005; Gross and Lodish, 2006; Nakajima et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from Corzo, 2006; González et al., 2005; Gross and Lodish, 2006; Nakajima et al., 2001.

claim: The p52:p52:Bcl3 complex preferentially recruits HDAC3 when it remains bound to an A/T-centric κB site.
source: We previously showed that the p52:p52:Bcl3 complex preferentially recruits HDAC3 when it remains bound to an A/T-centric κB site (Wang et al., 2012)
evidence: This is cited from the authors' previous work, Wang et al., 2012.

claim: It is possible that the slower dissociation rate or longer residence time of p52:p52:Bcl3 on the A/T-centric κB site matches the slower on rate of the corepressor to p52:p52:Bcl3 bound to A/T DNA.
source: it is possible that the slower dissociation rate or longer residence time of p52:p52:Bcl3 on the A/T-centric κB site described in this study matches the slower on rate of the corepressor to p52:p52:Bcl3 bound to A/T DNA.
evidence: This is speculation based on the kinetic data and previous findings.

claim: The A/T-centric κB DNA:p52:p52:Bcl3 complex remains stable for long enough to give the HDAC3 corepressor complex enough time to stably interact with it.
source: That is, the A/T-centric κB DNA:p52:p52:Bcl3 complex remains stable for long enough to give the HDAC3 corepressor complex enough time to stably interact with it.
evidence: This is speculation based on the kinetic data and previous findings.
